questions.explanation: Turner's syndrome females show short stature and underdeveloped feminine character including lack of secondary sexual characters.

questions.question: In which year was James Dewey Watson born?
questions.explanation: James Dewey Watson was born in Chicago on 6 April 1928.

questions.question: What degree did James Watson receive in 1947?
questions.explanation: In 1947, James Watson received his B.Sc. degree in Zoology.

questions.question: Where did James Watson receive his Ph.D. degree?
questions.explanation: James Watson received his Ph.D. degree from Indiana University, Bloomington in 1950.

questions.question: What was the topic of James Watson's Ph.D. thesis?
options: Effect of UV rays on bacteria
Effect of hard X-rays on bacteriophage
Effect of gamma rays on viruses
Effect of infrared rays on cells
questions.explanation: Watson's Ph.D. thesis was on the effect of hard X-rays on bacteriophage.

questions.question: When was Francis Harry Compton Crick born?
questions.explanation: Francis Harry Compton Crick was born on 8 June 1916 at Northampton, England.

questions.question: What subject did Francis Crick study at University College, London?
questions.explanation: Francis Crick studied physics at University College, London and obtained a B.Sc. in 1937.

questions.question: In which year did Francis Crick complete his Ph.D.?
questions.explanation: Francis Crick completed his Ph.D. in 1954 on a thesis about X-ray Diffraction of Polypeptides.

questions.question: What was the title of Francis Crick's Ph.D. thesis?
questions.explanation: Crick's Ph.D. thesis was entitled 'X-ray Diffraction: Polypeptides and Proteins'.

questions.question: In which year did Watson and Crick propose the double-helical structure for DNA?
questions.explanation: Watson and Crick proposed the double-helical structure for DNA early in March 1953.

questions.question: What was James Watson's age when he met Crick?
questions.explanation: Watson was a young man of 23 when he met Crick and they developed their friendship.

questions.question: When was Francis Crick made a Fellow of the Royal Society (F.R.S.)?
questions.explanation: Francis Crick was made a Fellow of the Royal Society (F.R.S.) in 1959.

questions.question: Which prize did Watson and Crick receive in 1959?
questions.explanation: Watson and Crick received the John Collins Warren Prize of the Massachusetts General Hospital in 1959.

questions.question: In which year did Watson and Crick receive the Lasker Award?
questions.explanation: Watson and Crick received the Lasker Award in 1960.

questions.question: In which year did Watson and Crick receive the Nobel Prize?
questions.explanation: Watson and Crick received the Nobel Prize in 1962 for their discovery of the DNA structure.

questions.question: What was the common interest that brought Watson and Crick together?
questions.explanation: Watson and Crick discovered their common interest in solving the DNA structure.

questions.question: How many serious efforts did Watson and Crick make before successfully proposing the DNA structure?
questions.explanation: Their first serious effort was unsatisfactory, but their second effort based on more experimental evidence resulted in the proposal of the DNA structure.

questions.question: What was the basis of Watson and Crick's second successful effort to determine DNA structure?
options: More experimental evidence and better appreciation of nucleic acid literature
questions.explanation: Their second effort was based upon more experimental evidence and better appreciation of the nucleic acid literature.

questions.question: Where was James Watson born?
questions.explanation: James Dewey Watson was born in Chicago.

questions.question: Where was Francis Crick born?
questions.explanation: Francis Harry Compton Crick was born at Northampton, England.

questions.question: What was James Watson's early interest that matured into a desire to learn genetics?
questions.explanation: During his early years, Watson's interest in bird-watching had matured into a serious desire to learn genetics.

questions.question: What is the phenotypic ratio observed in the F2 generation of incomplete dominance in snapdragon flower color?
questions.explanation: In incomplete dominance, the F2 generation shows a phenotypic ratio of 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, which is 1:2:1. This is because the heterozygous condition produces an intermediate phenotype (pink) rather than the dominant phenotype.

questions.question: In incomplete dominance, what is the genotype of the F1 generation when crossing true-breeding red (RR) and white (rr) snapdragon plants?
questions.explanation: The F1 generation produced from crossing RR (red) and rr (white) parents has the genotype Rr. Due to incomplete dominance, these plants show a pink phenotype instead of red.

questions.question: What is the genotypic ratio in the F2 generation of incomplete dominance in snapdragon?
questions.explanation: The genotypic ratio in the F2 generation of incomplete dominance is 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr, which equals 1:2:1. This is the same as the phenotypic ratio in this case.

questions.question: Which plant is used as a classic example to understand incomplete dominance?
questions.explanation: Snapdragon (Antirrhinum sp.) or dog flower is the classic example used to understand incomplete dominance. When true-breeding red (RR) and white (rr) plants are crossed, the F1 shows pink flowers (Rr).

questions.question: What does the modified allele produce in the first case of enzyme production explanation?
questions.explanation: In the first case, the modified allele produces the normal or less efficient enzyme, which is equivalent to the unmodified allele and results in the same phenotype.

questions.question: What happens when the modified allele produces a non-functional enzyme or no enzyme?
options: The dominant trait is always expressed
The phenotype depends only on the functioning of the unmodified allele
questions.explanation: When the modified allele produces a non-functional enzyme or no enzyme, the phenotype depends only on the functioning of the unmodified (dominant) allele. The recessive trait is seen only when both alleles are modified.

questions.question: What is the flower color of the F1 generation in incomplete dominance between red (RR) and white (rr) snapdragon?
questions.explanation: In incomplete dominance, the F1 generation (Rr) shows an intermediate phenotype. When red (RR) and white (rr) snapdragon plants are crossed, the F1 flowers are pink, which is intermediate between red and white.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a possible outcome of a modified allele in enzyme production?
questions.explanation: The text describes three possible outcomes of a modified allele: (i) normal or less efficient enzyme, (ii) non-functional enzyme, or (iii) no enzyme at all. A super-efficient enzyme is not mentioned.

questions.question: In the context of incomplete dominance, what does the term 'dominance' refer to?
options: Complete masking of one allele by another
Partial expression of both alleles resulting in an intermediate phenotype
Expression of only the recessive allele
questions.explanation: In incomplete dominance, neither allele is completely dominant. Instead, both alleles are partially expressed, resulting in an intermediate phenotype (like pink flowers from red and white parents).

questions.question: What is the phenotype of the parental generation (P generation) in the snapdragon incomplete dominance example?
questions.explanation: The parental generation consists of true-breeding red (RR) and true-breeding white (rr) snapdragon plants. Their phenotypes are red and white respectively.

questions.question: What is the genotype ratio of the F2 generation in incomplete dominance?
questions.explanation: The F2 genotype ratio in incomplete dominance is 1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr, which is 1:2:1. This is the same as the phenotypic ratio because the heterozygote shows a distinct intermediate phenotype.

questions.question: Why is the F2 phenotypic ratio different from the typical 3:1 ratio in incomplete dominance?
options: Because the dominant allele is completely masked
Because the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype
Because the recessive allele is completely dominant
Because there are three alleles involved
questions.explanation: In incomplete dominance, the F2 phenotypic ratio is 1:2:1 instead of 3:1 because the heterozygote (Rr) shows an intermediate phenotype (pink) that can be distinguished from both homozygotes (RR = red, rr = white).

questions.question: What is the key difference between complete dominance and incomplete dominance?
options: In complete dominance, the heterozygote shows the dominant phenotype; in incomplete dominance, it shows an intermediate phenotype
In complete dominance, there are only two phenotypes; in incomplete dominance, there are four
In complete dominance, the recessive allele is never expressed; in incomplete dominance, it is always expressed
In complete dominance, only one allele is present; in incomplete dominance, both alleles are present
questions.explanation: The key difference is that in complete dominance, the heterozygote shows the same phenotype as the dominant homozygote, while in incomplete dominance, the heterozygote shows an intermediate phenotype between the two parents.

questions.question: Which of the following best explains the concept of dominance at the molecular level?
options: The dominant allele always produces more protein than the recessive allele
The dominant allele produces a functional enzyme while the recessive allele may produce a non-functional or no enzyme
The dominant allele is always larger than the recessive allele
The dominant allele is always inherited from the father
questions.explanation: At the molecular level, dominance can be explained by enzyme production. The dominant (unmodified) allele produces a functional enzyme needed for a particular phenotype, while the recessive (modified) allele may produce a non-functional enzyme or no enzyme at all.

questions.question: What is the phenotype of the F2 generation snapdragon plant with genotype RR?
questions.explanation: In the F2 generation of incomplete dominance in snapdragon, plants with genotype RR have red flowers, plants with genotype Rr have pink flowers, and plants with genotype rr have white flowers.

questions.question: What is the phenotype of the F2 generation snapdragon plant with genotype rr?
questions.explanation: In the F2 generation of incomplete dominance, plants with genotype rr have white flowers, as this is the homozygous recessive condition that produces the original white phenotype.

questions.question: In the enzyme production example, what is the role of the substrate S?
options: It is the product of the enzyme reaction
It is the substance that the enzyme transforms
It is the gene that codes for the enzyme
questions.explanation: The substrate S is the substance that the normal enzyme transforms. The enzyme catalyzes the conversion of substrate S into a product, which contributes to the phenotype.

questions.question: What is the term for alleles that are slightly different forms of the same gene?
questions.explanation: Alleles are slightly different forms of the same gene that code for a pair of contrasting traits. For example, R and r are alleles that control flower color in snapdragon.

questions.question: In incomplete dominance, what happens when the F1 generation (Rr) is self-pollinated?
options: The F2 generation shows red, pink, and white in a 1:2:1 ratio
The F2 generation shows only red and white in a 3:1 ratio
questions.explanation: When the F1 generation (Rr) is self-pollinated, the F2 generation shows a phenotypic ratio of 1 red (RR) : 2 pink (Rr) : 1 white (rr), which is the characteristic ratio of incomplete dominance.

questions.question: What is the significance of the 1:2:1 ratio in incomplete dominance?
options: It shows that the dominant allele is completely masked
It shows that the genotype and phenotype ratios are the same
It shows that there are three alleles involved
It shows that the recessive allele is dominant
questions.explanation: In incomplete dominance, the 1:2:1 ratio is significant because both the genotypic ratio (1 RR : 2 Rr : 1 rr) and the phenotypic ratio (1 red : 2 pink : 1 white) are the same. This is because each genotype produces a distinct phenotype.

questions.question: In which year did Mendel publish his work on inheritance of characters?
questions.explanation: Mendel published his work on inheritance of characters in 1865.

questions.question: Mendel's work remained unrecognized until which year?
questions.explanation: Mendel's work remained unrecognized till 1900 due to several reasons including communication difficulties and lack of acceptance of his concepts.

questions.question: Which of the following was NOT a reason for Mendel's work remaining unrecognized?
options: Communication was not easy in those days
His concept of genes as stable discrete units was not accepted
He provided physical proof for the existence of factors
Using mathematics to explain biological phenomena was new and unacceptable
questions.explanation: Mendel could not provide any physical proof for the existence of factors or say what they were made of. This was actually a reason his work was not accepted, not something that helped recognition.

questions.question: How many scientists independently rediscovered Mendel's results in 1900?
questions.explanation: Three scientists - de Vries, Correns, and von Tschermak - independently rediscovered Mendel's results on the inheritance of characters in 1900.

questions.question: Which advancement helped scientists discover chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Advancements in microscopy allowed scientists to carefully observe cell division and discover structures in the nucleus called chromosomes.

questions.question: What are chromosomes literally called?
questions.explanation: Chromosomes are called colored bodies because they were visualized by staining. The word chromosome comes from Greek words meaning colored body.

questions.question: By which year was the chromosome movement during meiosis worked out?
questions.explanation: By 1902, the chromosome movement during meiosis had been worked out, allowing scientists to understand how chromosomes behave during cell division.

questions.question: Which scientists noted that the behavior of chromosomes was parallel to the behavior of genes?
questions.explanation: Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri noted that the behavior of chromosomes was parallel to the behavior of genes and used chromosome movement to explain Mendel's laws.

questions.question: According to the chromosomal theory, where are the two alleles of a gene pair located?
options: On homologous sites on homologous chromosomes
questions.explanation: The two alleles of a gene pair are located on homologous sites on homologous chromosomes. This is a key principle of the chromosomal theory of inheritance.

questions.question: What do chromosomes and genes have in common according to the text?
options: They both are found in cytoplasm
They both are visible only during mitosis
questions.explanation: Both chromosomes and genes occur in pairs. The two alleles of a gene pair are located on homologous sites on homologous chromosomes, showing the parallel behavior between genes and chromosomes.

questions.question: What is mutation defined as in genetics?
options: A phenomenon resulting in alteration of DNA sequences
questions.explanation: Mutation is defined as a phenomenon which results in alteration of DNA sequences and consequently results in changes in the genotype and the phenotype of an organism.

questions.question: Which of the following can cause mutations in organisms?
questions.explanation: UV radiations can cause mutations in organisms. These chemical and physical factors that induce mutations are referred to as mutagens.

questions.question: What is a point mutation?
options: Change in the entire chromosome structure
Change in a single base pair of DNA
questions.explanation: Point mutation arises due to change in a single base pair of DNA. A classical example of such a mutation is sickle cell anemia.

questions.question: What is pedigree analysis?
options: Analysis of family history about inheritance of a particular trait
questions.explanation: Pedigree analysis is the analysis of traits in several generations of a family to trace the inheritance of a particular trait, abnormality or disease.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a Mendelian disorder?
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is a chromosomal disorder, not a Mendelian disorder. Mendelian disorders are mainly determined by alteration or mutation in a single gene, such as Haemophilia, Cystic fibrosis, Sickle-cell anaemia, and Phenylketonuria.

questions.question: How are Mendelian disorders transmitted to offspring?
options: On the same lines as studied in the principle of inheritance
questions.explanation: Mendelian disorders are transmitted to the offspring on the same lines as studied in the principle of inheritance. The pattern of inheritance can be traced in a family by pedigree analysis.

questions.question: Which of the following is an X-linked recessive trait?
questions.explanation: Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive trait that shows transmission from carrier female to male progeny. Sickle-cell anaemia, Cystic fibrosis, and Phenylketonuria are autosomal disorders.

questions.question: What causes chromosomal aberrations?
options: Loss or gain of a segment of DNA
questions.explanation: Loss (deletions) or gain (insertion/duplication) of a segment of DNA result in alteration in chromosomes, leading to chromosomal aberrations. Since genes are located on chromosomes, alteration in chromosomes results in abnormalities.

questions.question: What are the factors that induce mutations called?
questions.explanation: The chemical and physical factors that induce mutations are referred to as mutagens. Examples include UV radiations and certain chemicals.

questions.question: What is the main carrier of genetic information in organisms?
questions.explanation: DNA is the carrier of genetic information. It is transmitted from one generation to the other without any change or alteration. However, changes do take place occasionally, which are called mutations.

questions.question: Which of the following is a chromosomal disorder?
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is a chromosomal disorder caused due to the presence of an additional copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy of 21). Haemophilia, Cystic fibrosis, and Phenylketonuria are Mendelian disorders.

questions.question: What is the inheritance pattern of sickle-cell anaemia?
questions.explanation: Sickle-cell anaemia is an autosome-linked recessive trait that can be transmitted from parents to offspring when both partners are carriers for the gene (heterozygous).

questions.question: What is the probability of a carrier mother passing haemophilia to her son?
questions.explanation: The heterozygous female (carrier) for haemophilia may transmit the disease to sons with 50% probability. This is because the son has a 50% chance of receiving the affected X chromosome from the mother.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of pedigree analysis in human genetics?
options: To trace the inheritance of a specific trait, abnormality or disease
questions.explanation: In human genetics, pedigree study provides a strong tool to trace the inheritance of a specific trait, abnormality or disease across generations in a family.

questions.question: Which disorder is caused by a mutation in the gene coding for phenyl alanine hydroxylase enzyme?
questions.explanation: Phenylketonuria is caused by mutation in the gene that codes for the enzyme phenyl alanine hydroxylase. This is an example of pleiotropy where a single gene mutation affects multiple phenotypes.

questions.question: What is the main difference between Mendelian and chromosomal disorders?
options: Mendelian disorders are caused by single gene mutations while chromosomal disorders involve whole chromosome changes
Mendelian disorders are more common than chromosomal disorders
Chromosomal disorders are always fatal while Mendelian disorders are not
questions.explanation: Mendelian disorders are mainly determined by alteration or mutation in a single gene. Chromosomal disorders are caused due to absence, excess, or abnormal arrangement of one or more chromosomes.

questions.question: What is the inheritance pattern of colour blindness?
questions.explanation: Colour blindness is a sex-linked recessive disorder due to defect in genes present in the X chromosome. It occurs in about 8% of males and only about 0.4% of females because males have only one X chromosome.

questions.question: What is the probability of a son being colour blind if his mother is a carrier?
questions.explanation: The son of a woman who carries the gene for colour blindness has a 50% chance of being colour blind. The mother is not herself colour blind because the gene is recessive and its effect is suppressed by her matching dominant normal gene.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about Thalassemia?
options: It is caused by a virus
It is an autosomal recessive blood disease
It is caused by excess iron in the blood
questions.explanation: Thalassemia is an autosome-linked recessive blood disease transmitted from parents to offspring when both partners are unaffected carriers for the gene. It is caused by reduced rate of synthesis of globin chains.

questions.question: What is the main characteristic of chromosomal disorders?
options: They are caused by single gene mutations
They involve changes in the number or structure of chromosomes
They are always inherited in a dominant pattern
They only affect the nervous system
questions.explanation: Chromosomal disorders are caused due to absence, excess, or abnormal arrangement of one or more chromosomes. This includes conditions like aneuploidy (gain or loss of chromosomes) and polyploidy (increase in whole set of chromosomes).

questions.question: What is the branch of biology that deals with inheritance and variation of characters from parents to offspring?
questions.explanation: Genetics is the branch of biology which scientifically deals with the inheritance and variation of characters from parents to offspring.

questions.question: What is the process by which characters are passed on from parent to progeny called?
questions.explanation: Inheritance is defined as the process by which characters are passed on from parent to progeny, and it forms the basis of heredity.

questions.question: What does variation refer to in genetics?
options: The exact copying of parental traits
The degree by which progeny differ from their parents
questions.explanation: Variation is defined as the degree by which progeny differ from their parents, representing differences in characteristics among offspring.

questions.question: When did humans first know that one cause of variation was hidden in sexual reproduction?
questions.explanation: According to the text, humans knew from as early as 8000-1000 B.C. that one of the causes of variation was hidden in sexual reproduction.

questions.question: What did early humans exploit from wild populations of plants and animals?
questions.explanation: Early humans exploited the natural variations present in wild populations to selectively breed organisms with desirable characters through artificial selection.

questions.question: Why does an elephant always give birth to a baby elephant and not some other animal?
options: Because of the principles of inheritance and heredity
questions.explanation: This phenomenon is explained by the principles of inheritance and heredity, where offspring inherit characteristics from their parents of the same species.

questions.question: What is the term for the process where humans selectively breed organisms with desirable characters?
questions.explanation: Artificial selection is the process where humans selectively breed and select for organisms that possess desirable characters from naturally occurring variations.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a question that genetics helps answer?
options: Why do siblings sometimes look similar or different?
What is the structure of a cell membrane?
questions.explanation: Genetics helps explain why siblings sometimes look so similar to each other or sometimes even so different, through the study of inheritance and variation.

questions.question: What is the basis of heredity according to the text?
questions.explanation: The text states that inheritance is the basis of heredity, as it is the process by which characters are passed from parents to offspring.

questions.question: What did Mendel's work and others who followed him help us understand?
questions.explanation: The work of Mendel and others who followed him gave us an idea of inheritance patterns, which forms the foundation of classical genetics.

questions.question: What is pedigree analysis?
options: A method to study family history about inheritance of a particular trait
A technique to modify genes in a laboratory
A process to create new species through breeding
A method to count chromosomes in a cell
questions.explanation: Pedigree analysis is the study of family history about inheritance of a particular trait, represented in a family tree over several generations.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a Mendelian disorder mentioned in the text?
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is a chromosomal disorder, not a Mendelian disorder. The Mendelian disorders mentioned are Haemophilia, Cystic fibrosis, Sickle-cell anaemia, Colour blindness, Phenylketonuria, and Thalassemia.

questions.question: What is the approximate percentage of males affected by colour blindness?
questions.explanation: Colour blindness occurs in about 8 percent of males and only about 0.4 percent of females because the genes are located on the X chromosome.

questions.question: Why is haemophilia called a sex-linked recessive disease?
options: It shows transmission from unaffected carrier female to male progeny
It is caused by a dominant gene on Y chromosome
questions.explanation: Haemophilia is a sex-linked recessive disease that shows transmission from unaffected carrier female to some of the male progeny.

questions.question: What type of inheritance pattern does sickle-cell anaemia follow?
questions.explanation: Sickle-cell anaemia is an autosome-linked recessive trait transmitted when both parents are carriers (heterozygous).

questions.question: Which amino acid is substituted in sickle-cell anaemia at the sixth position of beta globin chain?
questions.explanation: In sickle-cell anaemia, Glutamic acid is substituted by Valine at the sixth position of the beta globin chain of haemoglobin.

questions.question: What is the codon change in the beta globin gene that causes sickle-cell anaemia?
questions.explanation: The substitution of amino acid results from a single base substitution at the sixth codon of the beta globin gene from GAG to GUG.

questions.question: Which British monarch's family showed haemophilic descendants?
questions.explanation: The family pedigree of Queen Victoria shows a number of haemophilic descendants as she was a carrier of the disease.

questions.question: What is the probability of a son being colour blind if the mother carries the gene?
questions.explanation: The son of a woman who carries the gene has a 50 percent chance of being colour blind.

questions.question: What is the genotype of individuals who show the diseased phenotype in sickle-cell anaemia?
questions.explanation: Only homozygous individuals for HbS (HbS HbS) show the diseased phenotype. Heterozygous individuals (HbA HbS) are carriers but appear unaffected.

questions.question: What is the primary focus of the branch of biology known as Genetics?
options: Study of principles of inheritance and variation
questions.explanation: Genetics is defined as a branch of biology which deals with principles of inheritance and its practices.

questions.question: Who was the first scientist to systematically study the pattern of inheritance in pea plants?
questions.explanation: Mendel was the first to study the phenomenon of inheritance systematically while studying the pattern of inheritance in pea plants of contrasting characters.

questions.question: What term did Mendel originally use to describe the factors that regulate characters?
questions.explanation: Mendel proposed that the factors (later named as genes) regulating the characters are found in pairs known as alleles.

questions.question: What are the paired units of inheritance that regulate characters called?
questions.explanation: The factors (genes) regulating the characters are found in pairs known as alleles.

questions.question: According to the Law of Dominance, when are dominant characters expressed?
options: In both homozygous and heterozygous conditions
Neither in homozygous nor heterozygous condition
questions.explanation: The dominant characters are expressed when factors are in heterozygous condition and also in homozygous condition.

questions.question: Under what condition are recessive characters expressed according to Mendel's laws?
questions.explanation: The recessive characters are only expressed in homozygous conditions.

questions.question: Do characters blend in heterozygous condition according to Mendel's observations?
questions.explanation: The characters never blend in heterozygous condition according to Mendel's observations.

questions.question: What happens to a recessive character that was not expressed in heterozygous condition?
options: It may be expressed again when it becomes homozygous
It changes into a different character
questions.explanation: A recessive character that was not expressed in heterozygous condition may be expressed again when it becomes homozygous.

questions.question: What is the Law of Segregation?
options: Characters segregate while formation of gametes
questions.explanation: The Law of Segregation states that characters segregate while formation of gametes.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a type of dominance relationship mentioned in the summary?
questions.explanation: The summary mentions complete dominance, incomplete dominance, and co-dominance. Over-dominance is not mentioned.

questions.question: What does the Law of Independent Assortment state?
options: Factors assort and combine in all permutations and combinations
questions.explanation: When Mendel studied the inheritance of two characters together, it was found that the factors independently assort and combine in all permutations and combinations.

questions.question: What is a Punnett Square?
options: A square tabular form representing different combinations of gametes
questions.explanation: Different combinations of gametes are theoretically represented in a square tabular form known as Punnett Square.

questions.question: What is the term for the factors on chromosomes regulating characters?
questions.explanation: The factors (now known as gene) on chromosomes regulating the characters are called the genotype.

questions.question: What is the physical expression of characters called?
questions.explanation: The physical expression of the characters is called phenotype.

questions.question: What theory was developed after discovering that genes are located on chromosomes?
questions.explanation: After knowing that the genes are located on the chromosomes, a good correlation was drawn between Mendel's laws and the Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance was developed.

questions.question: Which process during meiosis was correlated with Mendel's laws of segregation and assortment?
questions.explanation: A good correlation was drawn between Mendel's laws: segregation and assortment of chromosomes during meiosis.

questions.question: What are genes located on the same chromosome called?
questions.explanation: Mendel's law of independent assortment does not hold true for the genes that were located on the same chromosomes. These genes were called as linked genes.

questions.question: How do closely located genes on the same chromosome behave?
questions.explanation: Closely located genes assorted together.

questions.question: How do distantly located genes on the same chromosome behave?
options: Due to recombination, they assort independently
questions.explanation: Distantly located genes, due to recombination, assorted independently.

questions.question: What do linkage maps correspond to?
options: Arrangement of proteins in a cell
Arrangement of genes on a chromosome
Arrangement of amino acids in protein
questions.explanation: Linkage maps corresponded to arrangement of genes on a chromosome.

questions.question: What are genes linked to sexes called?
questions.explanation: Many genes were linked to sexes also, and called as sex-linked genes.

questions.question: What are the chromosomes that are common in both sexes called?
questions.explanation: The two sexes were found to have a set of chromosomes which were common, and another set which was different. The common set was named as autosomes.

questions.question: What are the chromosomes that are different in two sexes called?
questions.explanation: The chromosomes which were different in two sexes were named as sex chromosomes.

questions.question: What is the sex chromosome composition of a normal human female?
questions.explanation: In humans, a normal female has 22 pairs of autosomes and a pair of sex chromosomes (XX).

questions.question: What is the sex chromosome composition of a normal human male?
questions.explanation: A male has 22 pairs of autosomes and a pair of sex chromosome as XY.

questions.question: What are the sex chromosomes in male chickens?
questions.explanation: In chicken, sex chromosomes in male are ZZ.

questions.question: What are the sex chromosomes in female chickens?
questions.explanation: In chicken, sex chromosomes in females are ZW.

questions.question: What is mutation defined as?
questions.explanation: Mutation is defined as change in the genetic material.

questions.question: What is a point mutation?
options: Change of a single base pair in DNA
questions.explanation: A point mutation is a change of a single base pair in DNA.

questions.question: Which disease is caused due to change of one base in the gene coding for beta-chain of hemoglobin?
questions.explanation: Sickle-cell anemia is caused due to change of one base in the gene coding for beta-chain of hemoglobin.

questions.question: How can inheritable mutations be studied?
options: By generating a pedigree of a family
questions.explanation: Inheritable mutations can be studied by generating a pedigree of a family.

questions.question: What is polyploidy?
options: Change in a single base pair
Change in whole set of chromosomes
questions.explanation: Some mutations involve changes in whole set of chromosomes (polyploidy).

questions.question: What is aneuploidy?
options: Change in whole set of chromosomes
Change in a subset of chromosome number
questions.explanation: Aneuploidy is change in a subset of chromosome number.

questions.question: What is the cause of Down's syndrome?
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is due to trisomy of chromosome 21, where there is an extra copy of chromosome 21 and consequently the total number of chromosome becomes 47.

questions.question: How many total chromosomes are present in a person with Down's syndrome?
questions.explanation: In Down's syndrome, the total number of chromosome becomes 47.

questions.question: What is the chromosomal composition in Turner's syndrome?
questions.explanation: In Turner's syndrome, one X chromosome is missing and the sex chromosome is as XO.

questions.question: What is the chromosomal composition in Klinefelter's syndrome?
questions.explanation: In Klinefelter's syndrome, the condition is XXY.

questions.question: How can chromosomal disorders like Down's, Turner's, and Klinefelter's syndromes be easily studied?
questions.explanation: These can be easily studied by analysis of Karyotypes.

questions.question: Which generation shows the expression of characters following a definite pattern according to Mendel?
options: Different first generations (F1), second (F2) and so on
questions.explanation: He observed that the expression of the characters in the offspring follow a definite pattern in different first generations (F1), second (F2) and so on.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the relationship between genotype and phenotype?
options: Genotype is the physical expression and phenotype is the genetic makeup
Genotype is the genetic makeup and phenotype is the physical expression
Genotype and phenotype are the same thing
Genotype is only found in plants and phenotype in animals
questions.explanation: The factors (genes) on chromosomes regulating the characters are called the genotype and the physical expression of the characters is called phenotype.

questions.question: In honey bees, how many chromosomes are present in a female?
questions.explanation: Female honey bees have 32 chromosomes because they develop from fertilized eggs and are diploid.

questions.question: How many chromosomes are present in a male honey bee (drone)?
questions.explanation: Male honey bees (drones) have 16 chromosomes because they develop from unfertilized eggs and are haploid.

questions.question: What type of sex-determination system is found in honey bees?
questions.explanation: Honey bees have a haplodiploid sex-determination system where females are diploid and males are haploid.

questions.question: In honey bees, how do males produce sperm?
questions.explanation: Male honey bees produce sperm by mitosis because they are haploid and do not undergo meiosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE about male honey bees?
questions.explanation: Male honey bees have no father, cannot have sons, but have a grandfather and can have grandsons.

questions.question: In honey bees, what develops from an unfertilized egg?
questions.explanation: In honey bees, unfertilized eggs develop into male drones through parthenogenesis.

questions.question: What is the term for development of an organism from an unfertilized egg?
questions.explanation: Parthenogenesis is the development of an organism from an unfertilized egg, as seen in honey bee males.

questions.question: In birds, which sex is heterogametic?
questions.explanation: In birds, females are heterogametic with ZW chromosomes while males are homogametic with ZZ chromosomes.

questions.question: What chromosomes do female birds possess?
questions.explanation: Female birds have ZW sex chromosomes, while male birds have ZZ chromosomes.

questions.question: In the ZW sex-determination system, which sex determines the sex of the offspring?
questions.explanation: In the ZW system, the female is heterogametic and determines the sex of the offspring, unlike the XY system where the male determines sex.

questions.question: How many pairs of autosomes are present in humans?
questions.explanation: Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes and one pair of sex chromosomes, making 23 pairs total.

questions.question: What is the sex chromosome composition in a normal human female?
questions.explanation: A normal human female has two X chromosomes (XX), while a male has one X and one Y chromosome (XY).

questions.question: What percentage of sperm carry the X chromosome in humans?
questions.explanation: During spermatogenesis, 50% of sperm carry the X chromosome and 50% carry the Y chromosome.

questions.question: If an ovum is fertilized by a sperm carrying the X chromosome, what is the sex of the offspring?
questions.explanation: When an X-bearing sperm fertilizes an ovum, the zygote develops into a female (XX).

questions.question: Which gamete determines the sex of the child in humans?
questions.explanation: The genetic makeup of the sperm determines the sex of the child because sperm can carry either X or Y chromosome.

questions.question: What is the probability of having a male child in each pregnancy?
questions.explanation: In each pregnancy, there is always a 50% probability of either a male or female child.

questions.question: What is the sex chromosome composition in a normal human male?
questions.explanation: A normal human male has one X and one Y chromosome (XY).

questions.question: In humans, what type of ovum is produced by females?
options: Ovum with both X and Y
Ovum with neither X nor Y
questions.explanation: Females produce only one type of ovum with an X chromosome.

questions.question: Which type of sex determination is found in grasshoppers?
questions.explanation: Grasshoppers have the XO type of sex determination where males have one X chromosome and no Y chromosome.

questions.question: What is the term for the sex determination system where males produce two different types of gametes?
questions.explanation: Male heterogamety refers to the system where males produce two different types of gametes, such as in humans and Drosophila.

questions.question: According to Mendel's Law of Dominance, which of the following statements is correct?
options: Recessive traits are expressed in heterozygous condition
Dominant traits are expressed only in homozygous condition
In a heterozygote, only the dominant allele is expressed phenotypically
Both alleles are equally expressed in heterozygous condition
questions.explanation: According to Mendel's Law of Dominance, when two alleles of a gene pair are different (heterozygous), only the dominant allele is expressed in the phenotype while the recessive allele remains hidden.

questions.question: What is the phenotypic ratio obtained in the F2 generation of a monohybrid cross between true-breeding tall (TT) and dwarf (tt) pea plants?
questions.explanation: In a monohybrid cross, the F2 generation shows a phenotypic ratio of 3 tall : 1 dwarf. The genotypic ratio is 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, but since both TT and Tt express the dominant tall phenotype, the phenotypic ratio becomes 3:1.

questions.question: A test cross is performed to determine the genotype of an organism showing a dominant phenotype. Which cross represents a test cross?
questions.explanation: A test cross involves crossing an organism with a dominant phenotype (but unknown genotype) with a homozygous recessive individual. For example, a tall plant (TT or Tt) is crossed with a dwarf plant (tt) to determine whether the tall plant is homozygous dominant or heterozygous.

questions.question: In snapdragon (Antirrhinum), when a true-breeding red-flowered plant (RR) is crossed with a true-breeding white-flowered plant (rr), what is the phenotype of the F1 generation?
questions.explanation: In incomplete dominance, the F1 heterozygote (Rr) shows an intermediate phenotype. In snapdragon, RR produces red flowers, rr produces white flowers, and Rr produces pink flowers - an intermediate between the two parents.

questions.question: In the ABO blood group system, when both IA and IB alleles are present together in an individual, what is the blood type?
questions.explanation: In co-dominance, both alleles express themselves equally. When IA and IB are present together (IAIB genotype), both A and B antigens are produced on the RBC surface, resulting in AB blood type. This is different from incomplete dominance where an intermediate phenotype appears.

questions.question: What is the phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation of a dihybrid cross between round yellow (RRYY) and wrinkled green (rryy) pea plants?
questions.explanation: In a dihybrid cross involving two pairs of contrasting traits, the F2 generation shows a phenotypic ratio of 9 round yellow : 3 round green : 3 wrinkled yellow : 1 wrinkled green. This is derived from (3:1) x (3:1) = 9:3:3:1, demonstrating the Law of Independent Assortment.

questions.question: Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment states that:
options: Alleles of the same gene segregate together
When two pairs of traits are combined, segregation of one pair is independent of the other pair
Dominant alleles always mask recessive alleles
Genes on the same chromosome always assort together
questions.explanation: The Law of Independent Assortment states that when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, the segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair. This means different genes are inherited independently of one another during gamete formation.

questions.question: The Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance was proposed by:
questions.explanation: Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri independently proposed the Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance in 1902. They noted that the behavior of chromosomes during meiosis was parallel to the behavior of genes, and used chromosome movement to explain Mendel's laws.

questions.question: In human beings, sex determination is of which type?
questions.explanation: Humans have XY type of sex determination. Males have 22 pairs of autosomes plus XY sex chromosomes, while females have 22 pairs of autosomes plus XX sex chromosomes. The male is heterogametic, producing 50% X-bearing and 50% Y-bearing sperm.

questions.question: In honey bees, males (drones) develop from:
questions.explanation: Honey bees show haplodiploid sex determination. Males (drones) develop from unfertilized eggs through parthenogenesis and are haploid (16 chromosomes). Females (queens and workers) develop from fertilized eggs and are diploid (32 chromosomes).

questions.question: Sickle cell anemia is caused by which type of mutation?
questions.explanation: Sickle cell anemia is caused by a point mutation - a change in a single base pair in the DNA. The sixth codon of the beta-globin gene is changed from GAG (glutamic acid) to GTG (valine), resulting in the production of abnormal hemoglobin (HbS).

questions.question: What is the main purpose of pedigree analysis in human genetics?
options: To determine the exact DNA sequence of an individual
To trace the inheritance pattern of a specific trait through generations
To measure mutation rates in populations
questions.explanation: Pedigree analysis is a tool used to trace the inheritance of a specific trait, abnormality, or disease through several generations of a family. It helps determine whether a trait is dominant or recessive, autosomal or sex-linked, and identifies carriers.

questions.question: Haemophilia is a sex-linked recessive disorder. Which statement about its inheritance is correct?
options: It is more common in females than males
An affected father cannot pass it to his sons
It is transmitted from affected father to all daughters
It can be inherited from both parents equally
questions.explanation: Haemophilia is an X-linked recessive disorder. An affected father (XhY) passes his X chromosome to all daughters (making them carriers) but his Y chromosome to sons. Therefore, an affected father cannot pass haemophilia to his sons. Sons can only inherit it from carrier mothers.

questions.question: Down's syndrome is caused by:
questions.explanation: Down's syndrome is caused by trisomy of chromosome 21, meaning there is an extra copy of chromosome 21. The total chromosome number becomes 47 instead of 46. This results in characteristic features including short stature, round head, furrowed tongue, and mental retardation.

questions.question: Human skin color is an example of:
questions.explanation: Human skin color is a classic example of polygenic inheritance, where a trait is controlled by three or more genes. The phenotype reflects the additive contribution of each allele, and environmental factors also influence the expression. The more dominant alleles present, the darker the skin color.

questions.question: Klinefelter's syndrome is characterized by which chromosomal composition?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter's syndrome is caused by the presence of an additional X chromosome, resulting in a karyotype of 47, XXY. The individual has overall masculine development but also shows feminine characteristics like breast development (gynaecomastia).

questions.question: Turner's syndrome results from:
options: Absence of one X chromosome (45, X0)
Presence of Y chromosome in females
questions.explanation: Turner's syndrome is caused by the absence of one X chromosome, resulting in a karyotype of 45, X0. Such females are sterile with rudimentary ovaries and lack secondary sexual characteristics.

questions.question: The ABO blood group system in humans is an example of:
questions.explanation: ABO blood grouping demonstrates both co-dominance (IA and IB both express when present together) and multiple alleles (three alleles: IA, IB, and i). IA and IB are co-dominant to each other but both are dominant over i.

questions.question: Phenylketonuria is an example of pleiotropy because:
options: It is caused by multiple genes
A single gene mutation affects multiple phenotypic traits
It is controlled by multiple alleles
questions.explanation: Pleiotropy occurs when a single gene influences multiple phenotypic traits. In phenylketonuria, a mutation in the gene coding for phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme leads to multiple effects: mental retardation, reduced hair and skin pigmentation, and accumulation of phenylpyruvic acid in urine.

questions.question: According to Mendel's Law of Segregation, during gamete formation:
options: Both alleles of a gene pair go into the same gamete
Alleles of different genes segregate independently
The two alleles of a gene pair separate and only one enters each gamete
Dominant and recessive alleles blend together
questions.explanation: The Law of Segregation states that during gamete formation, the two alleles of a gene pair separate (segregate) from each other so that each gamete receives only one allele. This is the basis for the 3:1 ratio in F2 generation.

questions.question: In Mendel's experiments, TT and Tt pea plants both appeared tall. This demonstrates that:
options: Genotype and phenotype are always identical
Different genotypes can produce the same phenotype
T and t are not alleles of the same gene
questions.explanation: TT (homozygous dominant) and Tt (heterozygous) have different genotypes but both express the tall phenotype because T is dominant over t. This shows that genotype (genetic makeup) and phenotype (observable traits) are not always the same.

questions.question: Thalassemia differs from sickle cell anemia in that:
options: Thalassemia is dominant while sickle cell is recessive
Thalassemia is a quantitative problem of synthesizing too few globin molecules while sickle cell is a qualitative problem
Thalassemia is caused by a point mutation while sickle cell is caused by chromosomal deletion
questions.explanation: Thalassemia is a quantitative problem - there is reduced synthesis of globin chains (alpha or beta), resulting in fewer normal hemoglobin molecules. Sickle cell anemia is a qualitative problem - a normal amount of hemoglobin is produced but it is functionally abnormal (HbS) due to a single amino acid substitution.

questions.question: T.H. Morgan's work with Drosophila showed that genes located on the same chromosome:
options: Are inherited together (linked) unless separated by crossing over
Follow Mendel's law of segregation but not independent assortment
Both B and C are correct
questions.explanation: Morgan discovered that genes on the same chromosome are linked and tend to be inherited together. However, distantly located genes can be separated by crossing over during meiosis, allowing for recombination. Closely linked genes show very low recombination frequency.

questions.question: Red-green colour blindness is more common in males than females because:
options: The gene is located on the Y chromosome
Males have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is sufficient to express the trait
Females are naturally immune to the disorder
The gene is dominant in males but recessive in females
questions.explanation: Colour blindness is an X-linked recessive disorder. Males have only one X chromosome (XY), so if they inherit the recessive allele on their single X, they will be colour blind. Females have two X chromosomes (XX), so they need two copies of the recessive allele to express the trait, making it much rarer.

questions.question: Mutation is defined as:
options: The process of crossing over between homologous chromosomes
A phenomenon that results in alteration of DNA sequences and changes in genotype and phenotype
The fusion of gametes during fertilization
The separation of alleles during meiosis
questions.explanation: Mutation is a phenomenon that results in alteration of DNA sequences, consequently leading to changes in the genotype and phenotype of an organism. Mutations can be caused by physical factors (UV radiation) or chemical factors (mutagens).

questions.question: Which seed colour was found to be dominant in Mendel's dihybrid cross between yellow round and green wrinkled pea plants?
questions.explanation: Yellow colour was dominant over green. Mendel found that the seeds resulting from crossing the parents had yellow coloured and round shaped seeds, indicating yellow dominance over green and round dominance over wrinkled.

questions.question: Which seed shape was dominant in Mendel's dihybrid cross experiment?
questions.explanation: Round shape was dominant over wrinkled. Mendel found that the F1 seeds resulting from the cross were round shaped, demonstrating that round is dominant over wrinkled.

questions.question: What were the genotypes of the parent plants in Mendel's dihybrid cross for seed colour and seed shape?
questions.explanation: The genotype of the parents was RRYY (round yellow) and rryy (wrinkled green). RRYY represents homozygous dominant for both traits, while rryy represents homozygous recessive for both traits.

questions.question: What is the genotype of the F1 hybrid produced from the dihybrid cross between RRYY and rryy parents?
questions.explanation: The gametes RY and ry unite on fertilisation to produce the F1 hybrid RrYy. This is a heterozygous genotype for both seed colour and seed shape traits.

questions.question: When Mendel self-hybridised the F1 plants (RrYy), what phenotypic ratio was observed for seed colour in the F2 generation?
questions.explanation: When Mendel self hybridised the F1 plants he found that 3/4th of F2 plants had yellow seeds and 1/4th had green. The yellow and green colour segregated in a 3:1 ratio, just like in a monohybrid cross.

questions.question: What was the phenotypic ratio for seed shape when F1 plants were self-hybridised?
questions.explanation: Round and wrinkled seed shape also segregated in a 3:1 ratio, just like in a monohybrid cross. This demonstrates independent segregation of each trait.

questions.question: Which genotypic symbol represents the dominant yellow seed colour in Mendel's dihybrid cross?
questions.explanation: Y is used for dominant yellow seed colour and y for recessive green seed colour. Capital letters represent dominant alleles while lowercase letters represent recessive alleles.

questions.question: What does the genotypic symbol 'r' represent in Mendel's dihybrid cross?
questions.explanation: R is used for round shaped seeds (dominant) and r for wrinkled seed shape (recessive). The lowercase r represents the recessive allele for wrinkled seed shape.

questions.question: What type of gametes are produced by the parent plant with genotype RRYY?
questions.explanation: The parent plant with genotype RRYY can only produce gametes containing RY because it is homozygous dominant for both traits. All gametes will carry the dominant alleles R and Y.

questions.question: What type of gametes are produced by the parent plant with genotype rryy?
questions.explanation: The parent plant with genotype rryy can only produce gametes containing ry because it is homozygous recessive for both traits. All gametes will carry the recessive alleles r and y.

questions.question: How did the results of the dihybrid cross compare to separate monohybrid crosses?
options: The dihybrid cross showed no segregation
The monohybrid crosses showed different ratios
questions.explanation: These results were identical to those that Mendel got when he made separate monohybrid crosses between yellow and green seeded plants and between round and wrinkled seeded plants. Each trait segregated independently in a 3:1 ratio.

questions.question: In the dihybrid cross, what fraction of F2 plants had green seeds when F1 was self-hybridised?
questions.explanation: When Mendel self hybridised the F1 plants he found that 3/4th of F2 plants had yellow seeds and 1/4th had green. Therefore, 1/4 of F2 plants had green seeds.

questions.question: What fraction of F2 plants had yellow seeds when F1 was self-hybridised?
questions.explanation: When Mendel self hybridised the F1 plants he found that 3/4th of F2 plants had yellow seeds. This demonstrates the dominance of yellow over green in a 3:1 phenotypic ratio.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the F1 phenotype in Mendel's dihybrid cross?
questions.explanation: Mendel found that the seeds resulting from the crossing of the parents had yellow coloured and round shaped seeds. The F1 phenotype was yellow and round because both yellow and round are dominant traits.

questions.question: What is the term for a cross involving two pairs of contrasting traits?
questions.explanation: A dihybrid cross involves two pairs of contrasting traits. In this case, Mendel crossed pea plants differing in seed colour (yellow/green) and seed shape (round/wrinkled), making it a dihybrid cross.

questions.question: The genotype RrYy is an example of which type of genotype?
questions.explanation: RrYy is heterozygous for both seed colour (Yy) and seed shape (Rr). It contains one dominant and one recessive allele for each trait, making it heterozygous for both traits.

questions.question: What happens when gametes RY and ry unite during fertilisation?
questions.explanation: The gametes RY and ry unite on fertilisation to produce the F1 hybrid RrYy. Each parent contributes one allele for each trait, resulting in a heterozygous genotype.

questions.question: Which trait pair was NOT studied by Mendel in the dihybrid cross described on this page?
options: Both A and B were studied
questions.explanation: On this page, Mendel studied seed colour (yellow/green) and seed shape (round/wrinkled) in the dihybrid cross. Tall and dwarf plant height was studied in monohybrid crosses, not in this particular dihybrid cross described on page 10.

questions.question: What does the capital letter Y represent in the genotypic notation?
questions.explanation: Y represents the dominant yellow seed colour allele. By convention, capital letters are used for dominant alleles and lowercase letters for recessive alleles.

questions.question: What does the lowercase letter y represent in the genotypic notation?
questions.explanation: y represents the recessive green seed colour allele. Lowercase letters are used for recessive alleles, while capital letters represent dominant alleles in genetic notation.

questions.question: In a dihybrid cross between pea plants with round yellow seeds (RRYY) and wrinkled green seeds (rryy), what is the phenotype of the F1 generation?
questions.explanation: When RRYY (round yellow) is crossed with rryy (wrinkled green), the F1 generation will have genotype RrYy. Since round (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r) and yellow (Y) is dominant over green (y), all F1 plants show the dominant phenotype which is round yellow seeds.

questions.question: What is the phenotypic ratio observed in the F2 generation of a dihybrid cross?
questions.explanation: In a dihybrid cross, the F2 generation shows a phenotypic ratio of 9:3:3:1. This means 9/16 round yellow, 3/16 wrinkled yellow, 3/16 round green, and 1/16 wrinkled green. This ratio is derived from combining two monohybrid ratios: (3 round:1 wrinkled) x (3 yellow:1 green) = 9:3:3:1.

questions.question: According to Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment, what happens when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid?
options: Segregation of one pair is independent of the other pair
Only one pair segregates at a time
The traits cancel each other out
questions.explanation: Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment states that when two pairs of traits are combined in a hybrid, segregation of one pair of characters is independent of the other pair of characters. This means the inheritance of one trait does not affect the inheritance of another trait.

questions.question: How many different genotypes of gametes are produced by an F1 plant with genotype RrYy?
questions.explanation: An F1 plant with genotype RrYy produces four types of gametes: RY, Ry, rY, and ry. Each gamete has a frequency of 25% or 1/4th of the total gametes produced. This is because the segregation of R/r is independent of the segregation of Y/y.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly represents the derivation of the 9:3:3:1 ratio?
questions.explanation: The 9:3:3:1 ratio is derived as a combination series of two monohybrid ratios: (3 Round:1 Wrinkled) x (3 Yellow:1 Green) = 9 Round Yellow:3 Wrinkled Yellow:3 Round Green:1 Wrinkled Green. This is a multiplication of probabilities, not addition.

questions.question: What percentage of gametes produced by an RrYy plant will carry the allele combination rY?
questions.explanation: The four gamete types (RY, Ry, rY, ry) are produced in equal proportions of 25% each. Since 50% of gametes carry r and 50% of those carry Y, the probability of rY is 0.5 x 0.5 = 0.25 or 25%.

questions.question: In the dihybrid cross, yellow seed color is dominant over green and round shape is dominant over wrinkled. What is the genotype of the parental plant with round yellow seeds?
questions.explanation: The parental plant with round yellow seeds is a true-breeding plant, so its genotype is homozygous dominant for both traits: RRYY. True-breeding plants are homozygous and produce offspring identical to themselves when self-pollinated.

questions.question: Mendel's work on inheritance was published in 1865 but remained unrecognized until 1900. Which of the following was NOT a reason for this?
options: Communication was difficult in those days
His mathematical approach was new and unacceptable
He provided physical proof for the existence of genes
His concept of discrete genes was not accepted by contemporaries
questions.explanation: Mendel could NOT provide any physical proof for the existence of factors (genes) or say what they were made of. This was one of the reasons his work was not immediately accepted. The other reasons included difficult communication, his mathematical approach being new, and his concept of discrete genes not being accepted.

questions.question: Who independently rediscovered Mendel's results on inheritance in 1900?
options: de Vries, Correns and von Tschermak
questions.explanation: In 1900, three scientists - de Vries, Correns, and von Tschermak - independently rediscovered Mendel's results on the inheritance of characters. This led to the recognition of Mendel's work as the foundation of genetics.

questions.question: What structures in the nucleus were discovered due to advancements in microscopy and appeared to double and divide before cell division?
questions.explanation: Due to advancements in microscopy, scientists discovered structures in the nucleus called chromosomes (colored bodies, as they were visualized by staining). These appeared to double and divide just before each cell division.

questions.question: Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri used what observation to explain Mendel's laws?
questions.explanation: Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri noted that the behavior of chromosomes was parallel to the behavior of genes and used chromosome movement during meiosis to explain Mendel's laws. This became known as the Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance.

questions.question: In the dihybrid cross Punnett square, how many squares are there in total for the F2 generation?
questions.explanation: The Punnett square for a dihybrid cross has 16 squares in total. This is because there are 4 types of gametes from each parent (RY, Ry, rY, ry), and 4 x 4 = 16 possible combinations in the F2 generation.

questions.question: What is the genotypic ratio of a monohybrid cross in the F2 generation?
questions.explanation: The genotypic ratio of a monohybrid cross in F2 is 1:2:1 (1 TT:2 Tt:1 tt). This is different from the phenotypic ratio of 3:1. The genotypic ratio shows the actual genetic makeup, while the phenotypic ratio shows the observable characteristics.

questions.question: If yellow color (Y) is dominant over green (y) and round shape (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r), what is the phenotype of a plant with genotype RrYY?
questions.explanation: A plant with genotype RrYY has one dominant allele for round (R) and is homozygous dominant for yellow (YY). Since R is dominant over r, the plant shows round seeds. Since YY is homozygous dominant, the plant shows yellow seeds. Therefore, the phenotype is round yellow.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between genes and chromosomes according to the Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance?
options: Genes and chromosomes have no relationship
Genes are located on chromosomes and their behavior is parallel
Genes and chromosomes behave in opposite ways
questions.explanation: According to the Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance, genes are located on chromosomes and the behavior of chromosomes is parallel to the behavior of genes. Both occur in pairs, segregate during gamete formation, and independent pairs segregate independently of each other.

questions.question: In the context of independent assortment, what is the probability that a gamete from an RrYy plant will contain both dominant alleles (RY)?
questions.explanation: The probability of a gamete containing R is 1/2, and the probability of containing Y is 1/2. Since these are independent events, the probability of both occurring together is 1/2 x 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.question: What is the frequency of each gamete type (RY, Ry, rY, ry) produced by an F1 RrYy plant?
questions.explanation: An F1 RrYy plant produces four types of gametes (RY, Ry, rY, ry) each with a frequency of 25% or 1/4th of the total gametes. This equal distribution occurs because segregation of each gene pair is independent and random.

questions.question: The Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance was proposed based on observations of which cellular process?
questions.explanation: The Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance was based on observations of chromosome movement during meiosis. Scientists observed that chromosomes segregate and assort independently during meiosis, paralleling Mendel's laws of segregation and independent assortment.

questions.question: In a dihybrid cross, if the two genes are on different chromosomes, what is the expected phenotypic ratio in F2?
questions.explanation: When two genes are on different chromosomes (unlinked), they assort independently according to Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment, producing the classic 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio in the F2 generation.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key feature that both chromosomes and genes share according to the Chromosomal Theory?
options: They both are made of protein
They both replicate by mitosis only
They both are found only in the cytoplasm
questions.explanation: Both chromosomes and genes occur in pairs. This is one of the key parallels that led to the Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance. They also both segregate during gamete formation and independent pairs segregate independently.

questions.question: During which stage of meiosis do chromosome pairs align independently at the metaphase plate?
questions.explanation: During Anaphase of meiosis I, the two chromosome pairs can align at the metaphase plate independently of each other. This is the stage where independent assortment occurs.

questions.question: What is the phenomenon called when chromosome pairs align independently during meiosis I?
questions.explanation: The independent alignment of chromosome pairs at the metaphase plate during meiosis I is called independent assortment. This is demonstrated in Figure 4.9 of the textbook.

questions.question: In Possibility I shown in Figure 4.9, which chromosomes segregate together?
questions.explanation: In the left column (Possibility I), orange and green chromosomes are segregating together during anaphase I of meiosis.

questions.question: In Possibility II shown in Figure 4.9, which chromosome segregates with the red chromosome?
questions.explanation: In the right hand column (Possibility II), the orange chromosome is segregating with the red chromosome during anaphase I.

questions.question: How many different possibilities of chromosome segregation are shown in Figure 4.9?
questions.explanation: Figure 4.9 shows two possibilities: Possibility I (left column) and Possibility II (right column), demonstrating independent assortment of chromosomes.

questions.question: What does the comparison between left and right columns in Figure 4.9 demonstrate?
questions.explanation: The comparison between the left column (Possibility I) and right column (Possibility II) demonstrates independent assortment of chromosomes during meiosis I.

questions.question: Which chromosomes are mentioned as having four different colours in Figure 4.9?
questions.explanation: The text mentions chromosomes of four different colours in the left and right columns, representing two pairs of homologous chromosomes that assort independently.

questions.question: What happens to the chromosome pairs during anaphase I of meiosis?
questions.explanation: During anaphase I of meiosis, the two chromosome pairs segregate independently of each other, demonstrating the law of independent assortment.

questions.question: The independent assortment of chromosomes shown in Figure 4.9 is related to which Mendelian law?
questions.explanation: The independent assortment of chromosomes during meiosis I, as shown in Figure 4.9, is the cellular basis of Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment.

questions.question: In Figure 4.9, what are the two columns labeled as?
questions.explanation: The two columns in Figure 4.9 are labeled as Possibility I (left column) and Possibility II (right column), showing different segregation patterns.

questions.question: What is polygenic inheritance?
options: Inheritance controlled by a single gene with two alleles
Inheritance controlled by three or more genes with additive effects
Inheritance where one gene affects multiple traits
Inheritance linked to sex chromosomes only
questions.explanation: Polygenic inheritance refers to traits controlled by three or more genes, where each allele contributes additively to the phenotype. Examples include human height and skin color.

questions.question: Which of the following is a classic example of polygenic inheritance in humans?
questions.explanation: Human skin color is a classic example of polygenic inheritance, controlled by multiple genes (A, B, C) with dominant forms producing dark skin and recessive forms producing light skin.

questions.question: In polygenic inheritance, how does each allele contribute to the phenotype?
options: Each allele has a dominant effect over others
Each allele contributes equally and additively
Recessive alleles suppress all dominant alleles
questions.explanation: In polygenic inheritance, the effect of each allele is additive. The phenotype reflects the contribution of each allele, creating a gradient of expression rather than distinct categories.

questions.question: What is pleiotropy?
options: Multiple genes affecting a single trait
A single gene affecting multiple phenotypic expressions
Inheritance of traits through sex chromosomes
Complete dominance of one allele over another
questions.explanation: Pleiotropy is when a single gene exhibits multiple phenotypic expressions. The underlying mechanism involves the effect of a gene on metabolic pathways contributing to different phenotypes.

questions.question: Which disease is given as an example of pleiotropy in the text?
questions.explanation: Phenylketonuria is the example of pleiotropy given in the text. It is caused by mutation in the gene coding for phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme, manifesting as mental retardation and reduced hair and skin pigmentation.

questions.question: Who first observed a specific nuclear structure during spermatogenesis that was later identified as the X chromosome?
questions.explanation: Henking (1891) traced a specific nuclear structure during spermatogenesis in insects and named it the X body, which was later identified as the X chromosome.

questions.question: In XO type sex determination, which sex has only one X chromosome?
questions.explanation: In XO type sex determination, males have only one X chromosome besides autosomes (XO), while females have a pair of X chromosomes (XX). Grasshopper is an example.

questions.question: In XY type sex determination found in humans, what determines the sex of the offspring?
options: The egg carries either X or Y chromosome
The sperm carries either X or Y chromosome
questions.explanation: In XY type sex determination, males produce two types of sperm: 50% with X chromosome and 50% with Y chromosome. The sex of the offspring is determined by which sperm fertilizes the egg.

questions.question: What is male heterogamety?
options: Females produce two types of gametes
Males produce two different types of gametes in terms of sex chromosomes
Sex is determined by environmental factors
questions.explanation: Male heterogamety refers to the condition where males produce two different types of gametes: some with X chromosome and some with Y chromosome (or without X in XO type). This is seen in humans and Drosophila.

questions.question: Which type of sex determination shows female heterogamety?
questions.explanation: In birds, female heterogamety is observed where females have ZW chromosomes and males have ZZ chromosomes. This is the opposite of male heterogamety in XY systems.

questions.question: What is the sex determination mechanism in honey bees called?
questions.explanation: Honey bees use the haplodiploid sex-determination system where females are diploid (32 chromosomes) and males are haploid (16 chromosomes). Males develop from unfertilized eggs through parthenogenesis.

questions.question: How many chromosomes do male honey bees have?
questions.explanation: Male honey bees (drones) are haploid and have 16 chromosomes, while female honey bees (queen and workers) are diploid with 32 chromosomes.

questions.question: Besides multiple genes, what other factor influences polygenic traits?
questions.explanation: Polygenic inheritance takes into account both the involvement of multiple genes and the influence of environment on the phenotype. This creates a range of possible expressions for traits like height and skin color.

questions.question: According to the text, which genotype would result in the darkest skin color?
questions.explanation: The genotype with all dominant alleles (AABBCC) will have the darkest skin color, while the genotype with all recessive alleles (aabbcc) will have the lightest skin color in polygenic inheritance.

questions.question: What is the underlying mechanism of pleiotropy in most cases?
options: Effect of multiple genes on one metabolic pathway
Effect of a gene on metabolic pathways contributing to different phenotypes
questions.explanation: The underlying mechanism of pleiotropy in most cases is the effect of a gene on metabolic pathways which contribute towards different phenotypes. A single gene mutation can affect multiple traits.

questions.question: What are sex chromosomes?
options: Chromosomes that determine the body size of an organism
Chromosomes that are different in the two sexes and determine sex
Chromosomes that carry only metabolic genes
Chromosomes that are identical in both sexes
questions.explanation: Sex chromosomes are the chromosomes that are different in the two sexes and are involved in sex determination. The rest of the chromosomes are called autosomes.

questions.question: What are autosomes?
options: Chromosomes that are identical in both sexes and not involved in sex determination
questions.explanation: Autosomes are the chromosomes that are identical in both sexes and are not involved in sex determination. In humans, 22 pairs are autosomes and 1 pair is sex chromosomes.

questions.question: In honey bees, how do male drones develop?
questions.explanation: In honey bees, male drones develop from unfertilized eggs through parthenogenesis. This means males have half the number of chromosomes compared to females and do not have a father.

questions.question: What is unique about male honey bee reproduction?
options: They produce both eggs and sperm
questions.explanation: Male honey bees produce sperm by mitosis (not meiosis) because they are haploid. They do not have a father and thus cannot have sons, but can have grandsons.

questions.question: What phenotype would a genotype with three dominant and three recessive alleles (AaBbCc) show?
questions.explanation: In polygenic inheritance, a genotype with three dominant alleles and three recessive alleles (AaBbCc) would show an intermediate skin color, as the effect of each allele is additive.

questions.question: How many alleles control the ABO blood grouping system in humans?
questions.explanation: The ABO blood groups are controlled by the gene I, which has three alleles: IA, IB, and i.

questions.question: Which alleles of the ABO blood group system show co-dominance?
questions.explanation: When IA and IB are present together, they both express their own types of sugars on the red blood cell surface, demonstrating co-dominance.

questions.question: What is the genotype of an individual with blood group AB?
questions.explanation: Blood group AB individuals have the genotype IAIB, where both IA and IB alleles are co-dominant and express simultaneously.

questions.question: What is the blood group phenotype when the genotype is IAi?
questions.explanation: IA is completely dominant over i, so when IA and i are present, only IA expresses, resulting in blood group A.

questions.question: How many different genotypes are possible for the ABO blood group system?
questions.explanation: There are six possible genotypes: IAIA, IAIB, IAi, IBIB, IBi, and ii.

questions.question: Which allele in the ABO system does not produce any sugar on the RBC surface?
questions.explanation: The allele i does not produce any sugar on the red blood cell surface, while IA and IB produce slightly different forms of sugar.

questions.question: What is the blood group phenotype when the genotype is ii?
questions.explanation: When both alleles are i (ii genotype), no sugar is produced on the RBC surface, resulting in blood group O.

questions.question: In the ABO system, what is the relationship between IA and i?
questions.explanation: IA is completely dominant over i, meaning when both are present, only IA expresses and blood group A is observed.

questions.question: What is the phenomenon called when a single gene has more than two alleles in a population?
questions.explanation: Multiple alleles refer to the presence of more than two alleles for a single gene in a population, such as the three alleles (IA, IB, i) for ABO blood groups.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of co-dominance?
questions.explanation: ABO blood grouping is a classic example of co-dominance where both IA and IB alleles express simultaneously when present together.

questions.question: In pea seeds, starch synthesis is controlled by one gene with two alleles B and b. What is the phenotype of BB homozygotes?
options: Wrinkled seeds with small starch grains
Round seeds with large starch grains
Round seeds with small starch grains
Wrinkled seeds with large starch grains
questions.explanation: BB homozygotes synthesize starch effectively and produce large starch grains, resulting in round seeds after maturation.

questions.question: What is the starch grain size in Bb heterozygotes for pea seed starch synthesis?
questions.explanation: Heterozygotes Bb produce starch grains of intermediate size, showing incomplete dominance when considering starch grain size as the phenotype.

questions.question: What is the seed shape of bb homozygotes in pea plants?
questions.explanation: bb homozygotes have lesser efficiency in starch synthesis and produce smaller starch grains, resulting in wrinkled seeds after maturation.

questions.question: When considering seed shape, what is the dominance relationship of B over b?
questions.explanation: When considering seed shape, B seems to be the dominant allele because heterozygotes Bb produce round seeds similar to BB homozygotes.

questions.question: What is the phenotypic ratio of F2 generation in incomplete dominance of snapdragon flower color?
questions.explanation: In incomplete dominance of snapdragon, the F2 phenotypic ratio is 1 red : 2 pink : 1 white, which is the same as the genotypic ratio.

questions.question: What is the genotype of pink flowers in snapdragon incomplete dominance?
questions.explanation: In snapdragon incomplete dominance, the heterozygote Rr has a pink phenotype intermediate between red (RR) and white (rr).

questions.question: If a person has blood group B, which of the following could be their genotype?
questions.explanation: Blood group B can result from either homozygous IBIB or heterozygous IBi genotype.

questions.question: What is the phenotypic ratio of F2 generation in a typical monohybrid cross with complete dominance?
questions.explanation: In a monohybrid cross with complete dominance, the F2 phenotypic ratio is 3 dominant : 1 recessive.

questions.question: Which blood group genotypes can produce gametes carrying the i allele?
questions.explanation: Genotypes IAi, IBi, and ii can all produce gametes carrying the i allele, while IAIA and IBIB cannot.

questions.question: What is the relationship between dominance and the phenotype examined?
options: Dominance is always complete regardless of phenotype
Dominance depends on the gene product and the phenotype chosen
Dominance is only determined by the genotype
Dominance is independent of environmental factors
questions.explanation: Dominance is not an autonomous feature of a gene; it depends on the gene product and the particular phenotype that we choose to examine.
